{"id": "20:76/q01", "question": "What are the Gardens of Eden?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q01/p1", "position": "They are gardens of permanent residence, the lofty ranks promised to believers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says there is no departure or end; al-Baghawī and Ibn Kathīr call them everlasting; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī gloss ʿadn as abiding residence. Al-Jishumī includes rivers beneath trees and buildings; al-Biqāʿī says the dwelling conditions are already prepared. Ibn Jurayj identifies the promised high ranks with Eden; al-Rāzī and Asad describe them as believers' lofty stations."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q02", "question": "How is 'Gardens of Eden' parsed with the preceding 'high ranks'?", "turns_on": "Whether the following circumstantial khālidīn has a grammatical governor.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q02/p1", "position": "It is an apposition to the preceding high ranks or degrees.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls jannāt nominative by apposition to al-darajāt (20:75; also mentions 9:72). Al-Ṭabrisī and Abū al-Baqāʾ argue that an implied 'they are gardens' leaves the circumstantial khālidīn without a governor, so the pause should not fall at al-darajāt al-ʿulā. Al-Ṭabrisī says the preceding adverbial predicate of ulāʾika raises the degrees and governs what follows. Ibn Kathīr cites 20:75; al-Burūsawī also makes the river clause circumstantial to the gardens."}, {"id": "20:76/q02/p2", "position": "It is an explanatory substitute for the high ranks.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow this alongside apposition; Abū al-Baqāʾ says this parse lets an implied abiding or the demonstrative's meaning govern khālidīn."}, {"id": "20:76/q02/p3", "position": "It is the predicate of an omitted subject, 'they are gardens.'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and Abū al-Baqāʾ identify this possible parse only to reject it: khālidīn would have no governing element."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q03", "question": "What do the rivers beneath the gardens refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q03/p1", "position": "Rivers run below the gardens and their trees, dwellings, chambers, couches, or grounds.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies trees and cites 2:25; al-Burūsawī says dwellings or trees. Al-Jishumī adds buildings. Al-Qurṭubī specifies rivers of wine, honey, milk, and water under chambers and couches. Al-Biqāʿī adds grounds and says a river flows wherever desired. Muqātil, al-Nasafī, and Asad describe flowing waters beneath the gardens without a more specific location."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q04", "question": "What is the grammatical role of the river clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q04/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to the gardens.", "reasons": "Al-Burūsawī and al-Ālūsī both parse the flowing-river clause as a ḥāl modifying the gardens."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q05", "question": "What does abiding in the gardens mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q05/p1", "position": "Their inhabitants remain there forever, without death, departure, or a fixed endpoint.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Yaḥyā explicitly deny death; Yaḥyā and al-Ṭabarī deny departure, and al-Ṭabarī says there is no defined endpoint, mentioning 2:162. Al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Nasafī and Asad affirm enduring residence."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q06", "question": "How is 'abiding therein' parsed and governed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q06/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to the people promised the gardens, governed by the demonstrative's sense or by their established abiding there.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī names the demonstrative's meaning or the notion of abiding as governor. Al-Burūsawī relates the phrase to those for whom the reward is established or indicated. Al-Ālūsī specifies the pronoun in lahum and either the sense of establishment or ulāʾika as governor; he reports Abū al-Baqāʾ calling it a prospective state. Al-Samīn also reports the implied abiding or demonstrative meaning."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q07", "question": "What does 'that' point to, and why use a distant demonstrative?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q07/p1", "position": "It points to the described lasting triumph and bliss; its distance expresses exaltation.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the referent is near in discourse but is elevated by the distant form. Al-Biqāʿī supplies the omitted antecedent as 'that immense lasting bliss'; al-Burūsawī refers it to the reward just described."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q08", "question": "What does 'reward' mean here compared with 'wage'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q08/p1", "position": "Jazāʾ is recompense for good or bad, with or without contract; ajr is beneficial payment under a contract or its analogue.", "reasons": "Al-Burūsawī states this distinction while identifying the recompense here as the gardens already described."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q09", "question": "What does purifying oneself mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase specifies confession of faith, deeds, removal of sin, or the word's broader sense of growth; several sources combine faith and deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q09/p1", "position": "Cleansing oneself of unbelief and sins through faith, obedience, and righteous conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī offers righteous or cleansed of disbelief and sins; al-Jishumī says deeds bring reward. Al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Burūsawī, and al-Ālūsī name disbelief and sins, often adding faith and obedience. Ibn Kathīr adds rejection of evil and shirk, sole worship of God, and belief in messengers' reports and commands. Al-Biqāʿī supplies faith and good works; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says true belief and righteous action constitute sound growth. Islāḥī adds ideological, practical, and moral purification through Qur'anic guidance; Asad calls it attaining purity."}, {"id": "20:76/q09/p2", "position": "It means believing in God or professing 'There is no god but God,' thereby leaving unbelief or associationism.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā gives belief alone. Al-Kalbī adds giving the alms of one's soul to the profession; other reports from al-Kalbī, Ibn ʿAbbās through al-ʿAṭāʾ, al-Zamakhsharī's Ibn ʿAbbās report, and al-Rāzī give the profession. Al-Wāḥidī al-Wajīz and al-Nasafī explicitly make it a departure from shirk. Al-Ālūsī uses Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss to support inclusion of a major sinner in the promise."}, {"id": "20:76/q09/p3", "position": "It means performing righteous deeds or choosing and carrying out pure obedience.", "reasons": "Qatādah says righteous deeds. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says obeying God and choosing the purest acts, with the form suggesting acquisition. Al-Ṭabrisī reports an intention to obey followed by action."}, {"id": "20:76/q09/p4", "position": "It means cleansing the self of sins by obedience and avoiding disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī al-Basīṭ adds seeking goodness and virtue; al-Baghawī and al-Zamakhsharī speak of removing sins or their stains."}, {"id": "20:76/q09/p5", "position": "The root means growth in goodness; tazakkī is seeking growth, or, in another gloss, purification.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī compares the increase to wealth growing through zakāt. Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes sound growth as a life of true belief and righteous action."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q10", "question": "How do deeds and divine mercy relate to this reward?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse makes deeds a condition of its promise, and how that relates to God's mercy.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q10/p1", "position": "The promised reward is tied to purification through faith and good deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the verse shows reward comes through deeds. Al-Biqāʿī, al-Burūsawī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Asad, and Islāḥī connect lasting recompense to faith and righteous practice. Islāḥī rejects the theologians' claim that deeds do not matter and compares Jewish false hopes in al-Baqarah, while affirming that Paradise's key remains with God."}, {"id": "20:76/q10/p2", "position": "People enter Paradise by God's mercy, while their deeds determine their ranks there.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī transmits this from the Prophet without grading the report."}, {"id": "20:76/q10/p3", "position": "Deeds are unimportant to entry into Paradise.", "reasons": "Islāḥī attributes this wishful claim to theologians and rejects it, saying the Qur'an makes no such promise and that the key remains with God."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q11", "question": "Do sinful believers have a share in Paradise or lesser ranks?", "turns_on": "The scope of 'criminal' and the conditional threat in 20:74, the place of forgiveness, and whether major sinners remain believers eligible for the promise.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q11/p1", "position": "Sinful believers whom God pardons may receive lesser ranks or gardens, and a major sinner can remain within the promise.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī infers lesser ranks from the highest ranks being assigned to believers with faith and deeds (20:75), and attributes sinners' admission to grace and mercy. Sunnis argue that 'criminal' in the preceding threat often means unbeliever, citing those questioned about Saqar and mockers of believers (74:41, 74:46, 83:29); forgiveness limits the threat, and the conditional need not be universal. Even granting opposing premises, a major sinner remains a believer who has done good works, against the Muʿtazilite intermediate station; accountable people are believers or unbelievers. Even if the highest promise excludes sinners, lesser ranks remain. Al-Ālūsī cites Ibn ʿAbbās's shahāda gloss in support."}, {"id": "20:76/q11/p2", "position": "A major sinner is a criminal under the preceding threat and is therefore certainly assigned Hell.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazilites derive 'criminal' from a root associated with cutting fruit, later used for reprehensible acts; they apply the threat to every such offender. Sunnis challenge the term's scope, possible forgiveness, and the universal reading of the conditional."}]}

h includes this promise and the preceding warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the register and parallel tellings mark a divine insertion, or the verses continue the magicians' address to Pharaoh.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q12/p1", "position": "They are the believing magicians' words to Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports a group reading the verses as the sorcerers' admonition explaining their choice; al-Nasafī reports the same. Al-Bayḍāwī allows this reading. Al-Ālūsī prefers it against al-Nīsābūrī's view. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects it because parallel accounts do not similarly narrate this speech."}, {"id": "20:76/q12/p2", "position": "They are God's own speech inserted into the story.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports that God addresses Muhammad to expose Pharaoh's evil, the sorcerers' virtue, and the story's warning. Al-Nasafī prefers direct divine speech; al-Bayḍāwī allows it. Islāḥī says the afterlife register suits God's majesty, differs from the surrounding speech, and recalls the insertion at 20:53–59. Ibn ʿĀshūr observes the interruption before the exodus and rejects the magicians' speech from parallel accounts. Al-Ālūsī reports the divine reading as contrasting Pharaoh's evil and magicians' good but prefers the other."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q13", "question": "If the magicians spoke of these gardens, how did they know about them?", "turns_on": "Whether their knowledge came through other believers or direct inspiration.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q13/p1", "position": "They may have heard the descriptions from Moses or Israelites in Egypt, including believers of Pharaoh's family.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this as a possible explanation conditional on the magicians being the speakers."}, {"id": "20:76/q13/p2", "position": "God may have inspired the magicians with this knowledge when they believed.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī allows this alongside their having heard the descriptions."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q14", "question": "What is reported about the magicians' fate after their belief?", "turns_on": "Whether Pharaoh's threatened punishment is established as having happened.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q14/p1", "position": "Their execution by Pharaoh is not established by the Qur'an or sound reports.", "reasons": "Al-Burūsawī reports this caution about whether Pharaoh carried out his threatened punishment."}, {"id": "20:76/q14/p2", "position": "They became martyrs by evening after beginning the day as magicians or unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Burūsawī cites Ibn ʿAbbās for 'magicians in the morning, martyrs by evening' and Bahr al-ʿUlūm for 'unbelievers in the morning, righteous martyrs by evening'; the opening descriptions vary. He also cites the Mathnawī's story that they honored Moses by inviting him to cast first and treats cited reports as support for their martyrdom and Pharaoh's crucifixion."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q15", "question": "What reports describe the recipients of Eden and the highest ranks?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different recipients and scenes, without a stated dispute.", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q15/p1", "position": "People raised in Islam and good deeds without sin receive a banner and enter Eden after recognizing their description.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: they are summoned at Resurrection, recognize the description, receive a banner, and follow it into the Gardens of Eden."}, {"id": "20:76/q15/p2", "position": "The highest ranks appear from below like a bright star; Abū Bakr and ʿUmar are among their people.", "reasons": "Al-Burūsawī cites a hadith, and al-Ālūsī cites Abū Saʿīd reporting the Prophet; neither note gives a grading."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q16", "question": "How does this promise function in the story and sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q16/p1", "position": "It answers Pharaoh's threats and promises by setting eternal reward against the criminal's fate.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says it makes the preceding conditional explicit and that the criminal's fate comes first to hasten an answer about the threatened punishment's severity and duration (20:71). Ṭabāṭabāʾī says faith and works oppose the criminal's fate and answer Pharaoh's threat and promise (20:71–72); the high ranks answer his promised closeness and eternal gardens answer his payment (7:113–14). Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the interruption an admonition and confirmation of the believers' words."}, {"id": "20:76/q16/p2", "position": "The promise consoles the Companions for persecution at the sūra's revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī applies the promise to their suffering."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q17", "question": "Where else are Eden and its rivers explained or mentioned?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q17/p1", "position": "These descriptions are explained or repeated in other Qur'anic passages.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says the phrase was explained in Sūrat Maryam and the rivers in another passage. Ibn ʿĀshūr refers back to his treatment at 9:72. The Study Quran lists other mentions of Eden at 13:23, 16:31, 18:31, 35:33, and 98:8."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q18", "question": "What spiritual conduct does the promise invite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q18/p1", "position": "Choose God, remove blameworthy and satanic traits, cultivate spiritual and divine qualities, and give wealth and life for the highest opening.", "reasons": "Al-Burūsawī gives this inward application of purification."}]}
{"id": "20:76/q19", "question": "What danger does Islāḥī see in rejecting Qur'anic guidance on purification?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:76/q19/p1", "position": "Pursuing religious purity without the Qur'an's guidance leads to extremism.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says that guidance addresses human pitfalls and concessions and links ideological, practical, and moral purification to the reward."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q01", "question": "What do God's exaltation, kingship and truth mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q01/p1", "position": "God is exalted above creation and false descriptions; His sovereignty and truth are absolute.", "reasons": "Yahya and Jishumi derive taʿālā from height, the latter naming the tafaʿala pattern. Muqatil contrasts false gods. Tabari, Wahidi, Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Biqai reject polytheist descriptions. Nasafi excludes bodily likeness; Razi says majesty exceeds imagination and intellect. Tabrisi and Baydawi contrast divine and created power, knowledge and speech. Bursevi argues from necessary cause to contingent effect. Qashani says His rule gives each its due. Asad renders Ultimate Sovereign and Ultimate Truth."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q02", "question": "What does al-Malik convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q02/p1", "position": "God alone holds complete, effective and enduring sovereignty; other kings depend on Him and lose their rule.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, cited by Wahidi, places reward and punishment in His hand. Qushayri says malik intensifies mālik and true kingship is unique creative power. Tabrisi says God owns both worlds. Razi says His rule never changes or derives from another. Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi cite effective commands, promises and threats. Ibn Ashur invokes 25:26 and a hadith challenging earthly kings, comparing Muawiya's address to Medina's scholars; Allah paired with King denotes all perfections. Asad renders Ultimate Sovereign."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q03", "question": "What does al-Haqq mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the title describes God's intrinsic reality or His rightful dominion; several sources allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q03/p1", "position": "God is intrinsically existent and true in essence and attributes, unlike false gods and changing creation.", "reasons": "Yahya calls al-Haqq a divine name. Qushayri compares the evil eye being true, meaning existent. Nasafi says God truly deserves divinity. Ibn Kathir extends truth to God's promise, threat, messengers, Paradise and Hell. Asad stresses eternal, immutable reality."}, {"id": "20:114/q03/p2", "position": "God possesses or establishes the right and truly deserves kingship.", "reasons": "Qushayri offers both possession and establishment and accepts all senses. Wahidi and Qurtubi say possessor of truth or right. Al-Raghib, cited by Alusi, says God creates according to wisdom. Ibn Ashur says His sovereignty admits no incapacity or subjection."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q04", "question": "Why is God glorified at this point?", "turns_on": "Whether the praise closes the immediate judgment and Quran discussion or the larger Moses account.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q04/p1", "position": "The opening concludes or responds to the preceding account of revelation, divine power, judgment and guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya sees a close to the judgment passage. Razi says the Quran is magnified before God. Biqai sees the book and preceding eloquence, knowledge, power and justice as grounds for praise. Ibn Ashur calls it an interjection thanking God for reforming guidance. Alusi says it evokes wonder. Tabatabai prefers the resurrection and judgment context."}, {"id": "20:114/q04/p2", "position": "It may close the entire Moses account.", "reasons": "Tabatabai presents this as an alternative to his preferred immediate connection."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q05", "question": "How does the prohibition connect to the preceding praise?", "turns_on": "How widely to draw the preceding discourse.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q05/p1", "position": "The praise of God and the Quran leads to instruction in attentive, reverent reception of revelation.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Nasafi call it an aside after mention of revelation. Biqai contrasts not turning away with rushing ahead. Alusi cites al-Tibi: the Sender's and Book's grandeur call for understanding without haste. Ibn Ashur links it to the Quran's reforming message."}, {"id": "20:114/q05/p2", "position": "The earlier discourse about the mountains ends here and a new address begi

ns.", "reasons": "Razi reports Abu Muslim locating its start at 20:105; Alusi reports an excursus interpretation."}, {"id": "20:114/q05/p3", "position": "It connects to an earlier command to make the earth dust.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports Abu Muslim's connection."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q06", "question": "What haste with the Quran is prohibited?", "turns_on": "Whether the haste concerns recitation during delivery, transmission or interpretation before clarification, desire for quicker descent, or later reading of the whole Quran.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q06/p1", "position": "The Prophet must not recite along with or ahead of Gabriel; he should listen until the current passage ends, then recite.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others say he repeated the opening or each word for fear of forgetting. Razi and Ibn Kathir say God would preserve and explain it; Biqai says attention improves retention, and Bursevi and Alusi say speaking could hide the next words. Baydawi calls this primary. Tabatabai accepts the recitation explanation but rejects fear of forgetting on infallibility grounds. Islahi accepts natural eagerness but rejects it as the warning's reason."}, {"id": "20:114/q06/p2", "position": "He should not recite, dictate, convey or interpret for others until the passage's meaning is clarified.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Abbas and Atiyya report the clarification gloss. Tabari locates it in dictation to a scribe. Ibn Atiyya reports waiting to write. Razi and Abu Muslim mention a later exception, condition or other specification; Jishumi cites Abu Ali on general and ambiguous wording. Alusi says early conveyance is lawful and rejects this reading; Tabatabai finds no support in the verse."}, {"id": "20:114/q06/p3", "position": "He should not ask or press for further revelation before God's appointed time.", "reasons": "Dahhak and others report Meccans and the bishop of Najran demanded answers in three days and rumors spread when revelation delayed. Ibn Ashur says zeal to reform his community led to yearning for quicker revelation but mere wishing is allowed. Islahi compares the Prophet's waiting for Quranic aid to a soldier awaiting supplies, citing 19:64-65. Tabatabai rejects the wording fit; Alusi finds the Najran account unconvincing."}, {"id": "20:114/q06/p4", "position": "Readers should avoid conclusions from isolated verses until the coordinated Quranic message is considered.", "reasons": "Asad extends the first address to every reader and invokes 25:32 and 75:16-19; Kuranyolu reports this."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q07", "question": "What occasion is reported for the prohibition?", "turns_on": "Which reported event explains the admonition and whether the account fits its wording and prophetic protection.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q07/p1", "position": "The Prophet repeated Gabriel's words from concern he would forget the revelation.", "reasons": "Versions describe repeating the opening or every word, and fearing Gabriel's departure or loss from memory. Ibn Kathir calls Ibn Abbas's account authentic. Suyuti prefers al-Suddi's account over a cause cited in Surat al-Nisa. Tabatabai rejects fear of forgetting as incompatible with infallibility; Islahi rejects it as the reason for the warning."}, {"id": "20:114/q07/p2", "position": "After a man struck his wife, she sought retaliation; the Prophet first ordered it, then waited until 4:34.", "reasons": "Some specify a slap to the face. Wahidi says the story does not fit except perhaps the prayer for knowledge; Razi calls it remote. Alusi and Tabatabai reject the connection, the latter saying neither verse fits."}, {"id": "20:114/q07/p3", "position": "Delayed answers to Meccans and the bishop of Najran stirred rumors and a wish for faster revelation.", "reasons": "Dahhak describes a three-day deadline and a rumor of defeat by Jews. Abu Hayyan attributes the report to Mawardi. Alusi reports it but finds it unconvincing."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q08", "question": "What must be completed before the Prophet proceeds?", "turns_on": "Whether completion is verbal delivery or subsequent clarification of meaning and rulings.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q08/p1", "position": "The recitation or delivery of the current portion by Gabriel must finish.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports al-Mufaddal's delivery gloss. Ibn Ashur specifies the portion then descending. Biqai says revelation arrives in measured stages, and Bursevi compares completion of a term in 10:11."}, {"id": "20:114/q08/p2", "position": "God's clarification of the text and its legal or interpretive meaning must arrive.", "reasons": "Qatada glosses completion as explanation. Al-Hasan includes obligations, limits, rulings, lawful and forbidden matters; Yahya says following the Quran means acting on these, citing 75:18. Razi allows textual completion or explanatory revelation because later exceptions and conditions may alter the opening. Jishumi says the ending may change earlier meaning."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q09", "question": "What does qaḍā mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q09/p1", "position": "It means to complete, finish or fully deliver revelation.", "reasons": "Damghani says qaḍā can complete a period or the revelation sent to someone. Bursevi compares 10:11; Ibn Ashur specifies the portion then descending."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q10", "question": "How is the completion verb read and parsed?", "turns_on": "The verb's person and voice determine whether revelation is passive subject or object of God's direct act; al-Aʿmash further differs in final vowel.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q10/p1", "position": "The common reading has passive yuqḍā and nominative waḥyuhu as passive subject.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls this the majority reading. Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Nashr explain its syntax. Durr reports al-Hasan reading this form. Biqai says the passive focuses on completion rather than naming the revealer."}, {"id": "20:114/q10/p2", "position": "Another reading has active first-person plural naqḍiya, with God as agent and waḥyahu accusative.", "reasons": "Yaqub, Ibn Masud, al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa and others are named, in varying lists. Thalabi specifies Yaqub's vowel pattern; Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi give kasra on dad and fatha on final ya. Qiraat-Er notes direct divine agency. Zajjaj says taqḍī is not read."}, {"id": "20:114/q10/p3", "position": "Al-Aʿmash reads active first-person plural with final yāʾ vowelless.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Lawami, quoted by Alusi, cite a dialect leaving final ya closed after kasra. Samin says this avoids a heavy movement on a weak letter and mentions 5:89."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q11", "question": "What variant pronunciation of al-Qurʾān is noted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q11/p1", "position": "Qurān without hamza simplifies qurʾān phonologically without changing meaning.", "reasons": "Qiraat-Er reports the omission."}]}
{"id": "20:114/q12", "question": "What lessons about judgment and action follow from waiting?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse imposes a rule on transmission and judgment or chiefly counsels receptive deliberation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:114/q12/p1", "position": "Withhold conveyance, belief or judgment until the text and any explanation or qualification are complete.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites Abu Ali on specification of general wording and explanation of ambiguity; an ending can change prior sense. Razi and Abu Muslim list private reading, delivery, apparent interpretation and public explanation, noting later exceptions and conditions. Qushayri advises testing outward evidence against foundations but applying general wording if no specific proof appears, against those who suspend judgment.
